lines.text: Palaces on Crete, the first democracy, the philosophers, an empire that lasted a thousand years and a nation reborn. This is the story of Greece.
On Crete, people settled at Knossos in the Stone Age, some nine thousand years ago. In time it would hold the grandest palace of the Bronze Age Aegean.
On the mainland, by around three thousand BCE, people were living at Athens, a city that tradition says took its name from the goddess Athena.
Back on Crete the Minoans flourished, with painted palaces, a script no one has yet read, and ships trading across the eastern Mediterranean.
By about sixteen hundred BCE, warrior kings ruled the mainland from fortresses like Mycenae. Their scribes wrote an early Greek, and their deeds became the tales of Troy.
Around then the volcano on Thera, today's Santorini, blew itself apart. It buried the town of Akrotiri and may have weakened Minoan Crete.
After the palaces fell, new city states rose. In the Peloponnese, Sparta raised its sons for war and was ruled by two kings at once.
At Delphi, on the slopes of Mount Parnassus, a priestess of Apollo answered the questions of cities and kings. To the Greeks, this was the centre of the world.
This was the age of ancient Greece, hundreds of independent cities around the Aegean, which gave the world democracy, drama and philosophy.
In 776 BCE the first Olympic Games were recorded at Olympia, in honour of Zeus. Every four years the athletes came, and the cities paused their wars.
Not long after, the poems we know as Homer's were taking shape. The Iliad and the Odyssey are the oldest great works of European literature.
In 508 BCE the reforms of Cleisthenes gave Athens a new kind of government. Its citizens met and voted on laws and war themselves. Democracy had begun.
Then Persia came. In 490 BCE the Athenians beat a Persian army on the plain of Marathon, and a messenger, the story goes, ran all the way home.
Ten years later the Persian king Xerxes returned with a vast army. At the pass of Thermopylae, Leonidas and his Spartans held it for days before they fell.
That same year, in the narrow strait of Salamis, the Greek fleet crushed the larger Persian one, and Greece was saved.
Now Athens entered its golden age. Socrates walked its streets asking hard questions about justice and virtue, until a jury condemned him to death.
Under Pericles, new temples rose on the Acropolis, the rocky hill above the city, which still crowns Athens today.
Its jewel was the Parthenon, a marble temple to Athena. It later served as a church and a mosque, until an explosion in 1687 left it a ruin.
Socrates' student Plato wrote dialogues like the Republic, asking how a city should best be governed.
In a grove outside Athens he founded the Academy. In one form or another, it taught for about nine centuries.
His greatest pupil, Aristotle, wrote on logic, ethics, politics and living things, and shaped thought for two thousand years. He also tutored a young prince.
That prince was Alexander of Macedon. He took the throne at twenty, conquered the Persian Empire and marched to India, and was dead at thirty two.
Centuries later Greece was part of Rome. When the empire split, its eastern half, ruled from Constantinople, spoke Greek, and lasted another thousand years.
Then Constantinople fell to the Ottomans, and Greece with it. In 1571, off western Greece, a Christian fleet defeated the Ottoman navy at Lepanto.
After nearly four centuries of Ottoman rule, Greeks rose in 1821. With help from Britain, France and Russia, they won their freedom.
In 1830 the modern Greek state was recognised, a small kingdom in the old lands of the ancient Greeks.
In 1896 the Olympics came home. The first modern Games were held in Athens, and a Greek runner, Spyridon Louis, won the marathon.
The twentieth century brought war and occupation. After the Second World War, Greeks fought each other, government against communists, until 1949.
In 1967 colonels seized power. Greece lived under a military dictatorship for seven years before democracy returned.
In 1968 Kyriakos Mitsotakis was born. He would become prime minister in 2019.
Alexis Tsipras, born in 1974, would lead the country through the hardest years of its debt crisis.
In 1981 Greece joined the European Community, tying its future to Europe.
In 2004 the Olympics returned to Athens. The shot put was held at ancient Olympia, and Michael Phelps won six gold medals in the pool.
Then, from 2009, the debt crisis struck, and Greece lived through ten hard years of cuts and bailouts.
In 2023 two trains collided head on near Tempi, the deadliest rail crash in Greek history, and the nation mourned.
From the palace of Knossos to modern Athens, Greece has carried its long story into every age.
